subject: dynamically forming function arguments to ggplot

messages.author: c8d747f3fcf42fea
messages.subject: dynamically forming function arguments to ggplot
parts:
I am wanting to form some (or all) of my arguments to qplot dynamically based on user input at the command line. I am dynamically generating the data set (query_results) from a database call and the string definition of main (title_str) based on the command line arguments. I could have several forms of qplot with various forms of the facet parameter and without it but I would be cleaner to generate this dynamically.

For example, at different times I need the following forms:
qplot(age, data = query_results, geom="histogram",
    binwidth = 1, facets = sex ~ colony, 
    main = title_str)

qplot(age, data = query_results, geom="histogram",
    binwidth = 1, facets = . ~ colony, 
    main = title_str)

qplot(age, data = query_results, geom="histogram",
    binwidth = 1, facets = sex ~ species, 
    main = title_str)

qplot(age, data = query_results, geom="histogram", # no facet parameter wanted
    binwidth = 1,
    main = title_str)

Mark

R. Mark Sharp, Ph.D.
msh...@sfbr.org

messages.subject: Re: dynamically forming function arguments to ggplot
parts:
Hi Mark,

I am a little unclear what your exact context is, but is this
something like what you want?

########################
foo <- function() {
require(ggplot2)

cat("Please type desired formula", fill = TRUE)
f <- scan(file = "", what = "character", nlines = 1, sep = "\t")
if (identical(length(f), 0L)) {
f <- . ~ .
} else {
f <- as.formula(f)
}

qplot(x = Sepal.Length, data = iris, geom = "histogram",
binwidth = 1, facets = f,
main = "My Title")
}
#########################

The logical test of f is probably rather unreliable, but you could use
the function like:

## use default, no facets
> foo()
Please type desired formula
1:
Read 0 items

## use facets
> foo()
Please type desired formula
1: . ~ Species
Read 1 item

It might help if you could give a little more information about what
your exact problem is (e.g., reading in data from the console, passing
strings as arguments, ....).

Cheers,

Josh

> Thank you for your kind help. This works great for all situations where I want an argument to facet, which is most of the time. However, the user may not need to use the facet option. Getting commands from the user is not a problem, I am just wanting to build the argument list to qplot dynamically and that means sometimes I want to have the facets argument and sometimes I do not.

Okay, then just set a default behavior (f <- . ~ . is the default in
qplot, i.e., no facet), and then if you want facetting, set facet =
TRUE, otherwise leave it as FALSE. I put it as an argument here, but
you could set the variable however you decide (e.g., whether there is
some factor or categorical variable, prior user input asking whether
they want facetting, etc.).

foo <- function(facet = FALSE) {
require(ggplot2)
if (facet) {

cat("Please type desired formula", fill = TRUE)
f <- scan(file = "", what = "character", nlines = 1, sep = "\t")

f <- as.formula(f)
}

qplot(x = Sepal.Length, data = iris, geom = "histogram",
binwidth = 1, facets = f, main = "My Title")
}

If you're writing a function to build ggplot objects, I'd recommend
working with ggplot() instead qplot() - qplot is not a good foundation
for this purpose because it's designed for the analyst to use, not the
programmer. However, reading the source code for qplot is very good
idea, as you'll see some of the tricks I use to try and make qplot
easy for an analyst to use.

Hadley

messages.author: 065110cca96a6373
messages.subject: Re: dynamically forming function arguments to ggplot
parts:
Mark,

I am glad to hear it. When you get a chance, I think the qplot code
will help you. One of the nice features of ggplot2 is that it is
flexible, and one of the ways it does this is building up graphs piece
by piece. Thus it is possible to do:

plot <- ggplot(data = iris, aes(x = Sepal.Length, y = Sepal.Width))

if (some condition) {
plot <- plot + geom_point()
}

if (some other condition) {
plot <- plot + facet_grid(. ~ Species)
}

if (more conditions) {
plot <- plot + geom_line()
}

print(plot)

If all the conditions were true, this would be equivalent (roughly) to:

ggplot(data = iris, aes(x = Sepal.Length, y = Sepal.Width)) +
geom_point() +
facet_grid(. ~ Species) +
geom_line()

or in qplot() terms (again roughly):

qplot(data = iris, x = Sepal.Length, y = Sepal.Width, facet = . ~
Species, geom = c("point", "line")). The "plot" object can be added
to or not, and then when you are all done (or at intermediary steps),
the final thing can be printed to the graphics device. This makes it
very easy to pick and choose what elements you want without having to
change much.

Cheers,

Josh
